title: Indexes and reading EXPLAIN
goal: By the end you can trace how lesson 4's B+tree turns a lookup into a few page reads, read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) node by node, choose the column order of a multicolumn index, say when an index alone can answer a query (heap or clustered table, INCLUDE, the visibility map), spot the function, cast or low selectivity that makes PostgreSQL ignore an index, and weigh what each index costs on writes.

warmup.q: payments has 1,000,000 rows in 23,818 pages of 8 KB. Card 4242 has 14 payments, spread over the table. With a B-tree index on card_id, the structure you built in lesson 4, about how many pages does PostgreSQL read to fetch them?
options: About 14: one per payment
About 17: a few index pages, then one table page per payment
About 1,100: the index is a twentieth of the table
All 23,818: an index helps sorting, not searching
warmup.why: The index is a tree three levels deep: one root page, one inner page and one leaf page lead to all 14 row addresses. Then each payment sits on its own table page. In the first Try it that is 3 + 14 = 17 buffers. The first option forgets the index's own pages; the third assumes the whole index is read, which only happens when the index cannot be searched.

sections.h: Lesson 4's B+tree finds 14 payments in 17 pages, where a scan reads 23,818
sections.body:
The support screen looks up one card's payments: `SELECT ... FROM payments WHERE card_id = 4242`. On the large data set, payments has 1,000,478 rows in 23,818 pages of 8 KB, 186 MB. Card 4242 has 14 payments. Without an index, PostgreSQL has one way to find them: read every page and test every row. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` runs the query and reports what it did (trimmed, estimates removed):

```postgresql
 Gather (actual time=22.943..249.431 rows=14.00 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=13203 read=10615
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on payments (actual time=15.929..233.812 rows=4.67 loops=3)
         Filter: (card_id = 4242)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 333488
```

Each line with a name is a node, one step of the plan. The sequential scan read the table from the first page to the last. Two helper processes and the main one shared the pages (`loops=3`; `rows=4.67` is the average per process, 14 in all), and each threw away 333,488 rows. A buffer is one 8 KB page: `hit` pages were already in shared_buffers (lesson 3), `read` pages came from the operating system. 23,818 pages for 14 rows: a quarter of a second here, and the cost grows with the table.

You built the fix in lesson 4: a B+tree. `CREATE INDEX payments_card_idx ON payments (card_id)` sorts all million `card_id` values, each with its row's ctid (lesson 2; card 4242's first payment is at `(339,35)`), and fills leaves from left to right. The result has the same three levels as lesson 4's `payments_pkey`: a root, 4 internal pages and 1,130 leaves. Lesson 4's index needed 2,733 leaves for a million keys, and this one needs 1,130 because card ids repeat. Since PostgreSQL 13 a leaf stores a repeated key once, with a sorted list of the ctids that have it, so card 1's entry carries 10 row addresses. Built with `deduplicate_items = off`, the same index takes 2,734 leaves and 21 MB instead of 9 MB.

Card 4242 now costs one descent through the root, an internal page and a leaf, then the 14 table pages its rows are on: 17 buffers and a quarter of a millisecond. In Kotlin terms:

```kotlin
val byCard = TreeMap<Long, MutableList<RowAddress>>()   // the index: sorted keys, row addresses
byCard[4242L]                                            // a seek: 3 pages, then 14 addresses
payments.filter { it.cardId == 4242L }                   // no index: test all 1,000,478 rows
```

That is the picture for this lesson: an index is a sorted copy of a few columns, each entry pointing to its row, and a query is fast when it can find **one short run of entries** in that copy. The rest of the lesson asks what lets a query find that run, and what the run costs once it is found.

sections.h: Read EXPLAIN from the innermost node out
sections.body:
A plan is a tree. Each node produces rows and hands them to the node above it, and the top node hands them to you. So read a plan from the most indented node upward, in the direction the rows flow. The stepper walks through the plan for card 4242's payments joined to their merchants, newest first. Four kinds of numbers tell you nearly everything:

- `rows` is what the node produced per loop, and `loops` is how many times it ran. Multiply them: the merchants Index Scan ran 14 times and found one row each time.
- `Buffers` counts pages for the node and everything under it. The Nested Loop's 59 is the payments side's 17 plus the merchants side's 42. The top node's buffers are the query's total.
- `cost=4.51..47.94 rows=11` is the planner's estimate, made before the query ran, in arbitrary units. Compare its rows with the actual rows. A miss by ten times or more means the plan was chosen from wrong numbers.
- `Index Cond` is a condition used to search the index. `Filter` is checked row by row after the rows were read, and `Rows Removed by Filter` counts the wasted work.

Three scan nodes come up all the time. An Index Scan follows each index entry to its row at once, in index order, which is how it can return rows already sorted. A Bitmap Index Scan first collects all the matching row addresses; the Bitmap Heap Scan above it sorts them by page and reads each table page once. PostgreSQL picks the bitmap when it expects more than a few rows, or rows spread over many pages: here, 14 rows on 14 different pages. An Index Only Scan answers from the index without touching the table; the fourth section explains when PostgreSQL can do one.

PostgreSQL 18 changed EXPLAIN in small ways you will see everywhere: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` includes buffer counts without being asked, rows have two decimals because they are averages over loops, and each index scan reports `Index Searches`, the number of times it descended the tree.

Plain `EXPLAIN` prints the estimates without running anything, so it is safe on any statement. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` really runs it: on an `UPDATE` it updates the rows, so wrap it in `BEGIN` and `ROLLBACK`.

sections.h: Column order decides which queries a multicolumn index serves
sections.body:
The merchant dashboard shows one merchant's newest payments in a month:

```sql
SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments
WHERE merchant_id = 1000 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
```

Without an index, PostgreSQL reads all 23,818 pages and sorts merchant 1000's 22 September payments: about 0.7 seconds. An index on both columns fixes it, but the order of the columns matters. A multicolumn index sorts by its first column, and by the second only among entries with the same first column, like a phone book sorted by surname and then by first name.

With `(created_at, merchant_id)`, September is one long run of about 100,000 entries from every merchant, sorted by time. Merchant 1000's entries are scattered through it. PostgreSQL walks the run backward from 1 October and checks each entry's merchant until it has 20: 397 pages, 11 ms.

With `(merchant_id, created_at)`, all of merchant 1000's entries sit together, already in time order, and its September is one short stretch. PostgreSQL descends to the last of them and reads 20 entries backward: 23 pages, a tenth of a millisecond. Both plans list both columns under `Index Cond`, so judge them by their buffers. The rule: **equality columns first, then the column you range over or sort by**. In Kotlin terms it is a `TreeMap` keyed by `compareBy({ it.merchantId }, { it.createdAt })`, where the range from (1000, 1 September) to (1000, 1 October) is one contiguous `subMap`. Swap the key's parts and no contiguous slice holds just merchant 1000.

PostgreSQL 18 softens the rule with skip scan, which lesson 4 ran on a four-region table. An index on `(status, created_at)` used to be useless for a query on `created_at` alone, because `created_at` is sorted only inside each status. Now PostgreSQL jumps into each status's part of the index and searches `created_at` there. For five minutes of payments it reported `Index Searches: 7` and read 27 pages, where a sequential scan reads 23,818. It pays off only when the leading column has few distinct values: through `(merchant_id, created_at)` the same query took 1,616 searches and 5,243 pages.

The third plan in the Try it reads 4 pages and never touches the table: an Index Only Scan, through an index with extra `INCLUDE` columns. The fourth section explains what makes that possible.

sections.h: Where the row lives decides whether the table is read at all
sections.body:
Card 4242's lookup in the first section ended in the table: 14 table pages for 14 payments. That comes from where PostgreSQL keeps rows. Its tables are heaps (lesson 2), and every index, the primary key included, holds ctids that point into the heap. A lookup is a descent plus one heap page per row, through any index.

InnoDB, MySQL's engine, makes the other choice, as lesson 4's compare showed. Its table is a **clustered index**: the leaves of the primary key's B+tree hold the rows themselves, so a lookup or range by primary key ends in the leaf. A secondary index stores the primary key instead of an address, so a lookup through it descends two trees, and a wide primary key such as a UUID makes every secondary index bigger. Writes differ too. A PostgreSQL update that changes an indexed column, or can't fit the new version on the same page, is not a HOT update (lesson 2), so every index gets a new entry, even indexes on columns that didn't change. An InnoDB update that changes no indexed column touches only the clustered index, because the secondary entries point at a primary key that didn't move.

Either way, a query can skip the row if the index already holds every column it needs. `CREATE INDEX ON payments (merchant_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount_minor)` keeps `amount_minor` in each leaf entry without sorting by it, and a merchant's total can run as an **Index Only Scan**.

The catch is visibility. An index entry can't tell whether its row version is visible to your transaction; that lives in the heap tuple's `t_xmin` and `t_xmax` (lesson 2). So PostgreSQL keeps a **visibility map**, two bits per heap page, one of which says every row on the page is visible to everyone. Only VACUUM sets it, and any change to the page clears it. An index-only scan skips the heap only for pages with the bit set, and `Heap Fetches` counts the rows it had to check there. InnoDB has the same problem: when a secondary index page was changed by a transaction newer than your snapshot, it looks the row up in the clustered index.

The Try it pays for three indexes on a fresh copy of 200,000 payments: the copy writes 89 MB of WAL instead of 42 MB. Before VACUUM no page is all-visible, and the planner doesn't even try an index-only scan. After VACUUM the merchant's total reads 4 index pages.

sections.h: PostgreSQL cannot search an index for a value it has to compute
sections.body:
An index on `created_at` is sorted by `created_at`. It is not sorted by `created_at::date`, or `lower(email)`, or anything else computed from the column, so PostgreSQL cannot search it for those values. Queries that look harmless hit this all the time.

`WHERE created_at::date = '2026-09-01'` read the whole index on `created_at`, 2,739 pages, casting each value and filtering: the plan says `Filter`, not `Index Cond`. The same day as a range on the bare column, `created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-02'`, read 13 pages. A condition that can search an index is called sargable, from "search argument". Keep the column alone on one side and put the computation on the constants.

The cast can come from your own code. PostgreSQL compares a `bigint` with a `numeric` by converting the bigint, so `WHERE payment_id = $1` with a numeric parameter, which is what JDBC's `setBigDecimal` sends, runs as `(payment_id)::numeric = $1`. The primary key goes unused and one lookup by id reads all 23,818 pages. Bind ids with `setLong`. Oracle has the same trap when a `VARCHAR2` column meets an `NVARCHAR` bind.

When you cannot change the query, index the expression. `CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email))` turns the case-insensitive login lookup from 532 pages into 4. The expression must be immutable, always the same result for the same input. `created_at::date` is not, since its result depends on the session's `TimeZone`, so PostgreSQL refuses to index it.

Sometimes the planner skips an index on purpose. 93% of payments are `succeeded`, so `WHERE status = 'succeeded'` needs almost every table page anyway. Reading the table straight through beats jumping between index and table 930,000 times, and the plan is a sequential scan even with an index on `status`. The same index is used for `status = 'pending'`, 1% of rows. If only the rare value is ever queried, a partial index stores only those rows: `CREATE INDEX ON payments (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` is 232 kB, against 21 MB for an index on `created_at` over every payment. The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove, while planning, that the query's WHERE implies the index's: `status = 'pending'` written in the query does, but `status = $1` in a prepared statement's generic plan doesn't, because the value isn't known yet.

Which indexes are worth their write cost? Ask `pg_stat_statements`, which the course's Compose service preloads. It groups each statement with its constants replaced by `$1` and records calls, total time and pages touched. Sort it by `total_exec_time`, `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` the top query, and build the index whose leading columns are its equality conditions. Then look the other way: an index whose `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` is still 0 after a month of traffic only costs writes. And PostgreSQL never indexes a foreign key's referencing column for you; without an index on `payments.merchant_id`, deleting a merchant scans payments.

refs.title: Use The Index, Luke: Functions in the WHERE clause

analogy: An index is the index at the back of a book. To find every page that mentions "chargeback" you do not read the book; you look the word up in the alphabetical list, which sends you to pages 12, 87 and 340. A multicolumn index is a list sorted by chapter and then by word: it finds "chargeback in chapter 4" at once, but not "chargeback in any chapter", because that word is scattered through every chapter's section. A partial index covers only the words of one chapter, an index on an expression lists the words in lower case, and a covering index also prints the sentence next to each entry so you never open the page. The analogy breaks on cost: a printed index is written once, while a database index is rewritten on every INSERT and every UPDATE of its columns, and PostgreSQL decides for itself, by estimates, whether looking something up is cheaper than reading straight through.
in_your_world: Most slow endpoints in a payments service are one missing or misordered index away from fast: the merchant dashboard (merchant_id, created_at), the card history (card_id, created_at), the idempotency lookup on payment_uid, the outbox poller on (status, created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'. pg_stat_statements is the place to start, and on Oracle the same question is answered by AWR's SQL ordered by elapsed time. Watch the JVM side for the hidden cast: a Kotlin BigDecimal id bound with setBigDecimal, or a Hibernate mapping of a NUMBER column to BigDecimal, makes PostgreSQL convert the column and skip the primary key. Every index also slows the Kafka consumer that inserts payments at 5,000 a second and grows the WAL that your replicas must replay and your CDC pipeline (Debezium) must read through, so drop indexes that pg_stat_user_indexes says nobody uses. In production, build them with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which does not block writes, in a Flyway migration that does not run inside a transaction.
mistake: Adding an index and assuming the query uses it, without reading the plan. People do it because the index exists, the column is in the WHERE clause, and the query got faster in development on a few hundred rows, where every plan is fast. In production the condition casts the column (created_at::date, a numeric bind on a bigint key), the columns are in the wrong order for the equality and range conditions, or the value matches most of the table, and the plan is still a sequential scan or a full index scan behind a Filter. The fix is to read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on production-sized data: the condition should appear as an Index Cond, the buffers should be in the tens rather than the thousands, and rows removed by filter should be near zero.

ORDER BY created_at DESC
FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;

-- the plan of this session's last statement, with
-- E-Rows (estimated), A-Rows (actual) and Buffers
SELECT *
FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));

b.title: PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
b.src:
-- runs the query and prints the plan with estimated
-- and actual rows, loops and buffers on every node
-- (BUFFERS is included by default since PostgreSQL 18)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, created_at
FROM payments
WHERE merchant_id = 1000
  AND created_at >= '2026-09-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- plain EXPLAIN: estimates only, nothing runs

compare.note: Both databases separate the estimate from the measurement. Oracle's EXPLAIN PLAN, like PostgreSQL's plain EXPLAIN, shows only what the optimizer expects; the actual rows and buffers come from running the statement with statistics collection on and reading the cursor's plan with DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR, where E-Rows against A-Rows plays the role of PostgreSQL's rows=11 against actual rows=14.00. Both print a tree as indented operations, read from the innermost outward. The index rules carry over: Oracle B-tree indexes follow the same column-order rule, Oracle has had an INDEX SKIP SCAN for many releases, its function-based indexes are PostgreSQL's expression indexes, and since Oracle has no INCLUDE clause, a covering index there simply adds the extra columns to the key.

worked.title: An index for the account statement, from a slow query to an Index Only Scan

steps.say: The statement page lists one account's ledger entries for a month, oldest first. pg_stat_statements puts it near the top by total time. On the large data set the ledger has 3,398,299 rows in 33,630 pages, and the plan reads all of them to return 4:
steps.code:
-- 1. the query and its plan (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF), trimmed)
SELECT created_at, entry_type, amount_minor
FROM ledger_entries
WHERE account_id = 4242
  AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY created_at;

--  Sort (actual time=224.879..229.448 rows=4.00 loops=1)
--    Buffers: shared hit=285 read=33348
--    ->  Gather
--          ->  Parallel Seq Scan on ledger_entries (... rows=1.33 loops=3)
--                Filter: ((created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...) AND (account_id = 4242))
--                Rows Removed by Filter: 1132826

steps.say: Choose the key from the conditions. `account_id` is an equality, so it goes first. `created_at` is both the range and the sort order, so it goes second: then the month is one contiguous run, already in the order the page wants, and the Sort disappears.

The query also returns `entry_type` and `amount_minor`. Each one found through the index would still cost a visit to a table page. Carry them in the leaf entries with INCLUDE, so the index alone answers the query.
steps.code:
-- 3. the same key, plus the returned columns in the leaves
CREATE INDEX ledger_account_created_idx
    ON ledger_entries (account_id, created_at)
    INCLUDE (entry_type, amount_minor);

steps.say: Check the plan, not the clock: an Index Only Scan with both conditions in `Index Cond`, no Sort, no Filter, `Heap Fetches: 0` and 7 buffers instead of 33,633. The bill comes with it: on the large data set the index is 161 MB next to a 263 MB table, written on every ledger insert. For a page every customer opens, that is a fair price. For a report run once a month, it is not.
steps.code:
-- 4. the new plan (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF), trimmed)
--  Index Only Scan using ledger_account_created_idx on ledger_entries (actual time=7.463..7.468 rows=4.00 loops=1)
--    Index Cond: ((account_id = 4242) AND (created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...))
--    Heap Fetches: 0
--    Index Searches: 1
--    Buffers: shared hit=4 read=3

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('ledger_account_created_idx')) AS idx,   -- 161 MB
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('ledger_entries')) AS tbl;              -- 263 MB

lab.title: Three indexes and one rewrite, checked against the plan
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. Five of the seven fail. The two that check the rows of `payments_on_day` already pass: its placeholder returns the right rows, the slow way.

The tests build a 200,000-row copy of payments once (schema `lab11`, vacuumed), run your statement on it inside a transaction that is rolled back, and read `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`. A failure prints the whole plan.
`merchant_month_index.sql` builds an index with the right columns in the wrong order. Fix the order so the dashboard query reads at most 40 buffers, with no Sort.
`payments_on_day.sql` casts `created_at` to a date. Rewrite the condition so an index on `created_at` can search it, keeping both edges of the day right.

`merchant_gross_index.sql` builds an index that finds the rows but cannot answer the query alone. Make the monthly statement an Index Only Scan with `Heap Fetches: 0`. Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Equality first: `CREATE INDEX payments_merchant_month_idx ON payments (merchant_id, created_at);`. Read the failing plan's buffers before and after.
`WHERE created_at >= timestamptz '2026-03-12 00:00+00' AND created_at < timestamptz '2026-03-13 00:00+00'`: half-open, so midnight is in, 23:59:59.5 is in, and the 13th is out.

The query reads `merchant_id`, `created_at`, `status` and `amount_minor`. Keep the first two as the key and add `INCLUDE (status, amount_minor)`. The second test adds five rows on a page VACUUM has not seen, so a few heap fetches are expected there.

drill.title: Pick the index, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the index for each query and say which plan node you expect. (1) `WHERE card_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10`. (2) `WHERE lower(email) = lower(?)` on customers. (3) `WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'`, where 1% of payments are pending. (4) `SELECT sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = ? AND created_at >= ? AND created_at < ?`. Then rewrite `WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-03-12'` so an index on created_at can serve it.

recap: An index is lesson 4's B+tree over a few columns, each entry holding its row's address. Three levels find card 4242's entries in 3 page reads, then one table page per row; without it, PostgreSQL reads all 23,818 pages.
Read EXPLAIN from the most indented node up. rows is per loop, so multiply by loops; Buffers include the children; compare estimated rows with actual rows; Index Cond searches, Filter only discards.
In a multicolumn index, equality columns come first, then the range or sort column. PostgreSQL 18's skip scan helps only when the leading column has few distinct values.

PostgreSQL indexes point into a heap; InnoDB's secondary indexes hold the primary key and descend the clustered index. INCLUDE columns allow an Index Only Scan, which skips only the pages VACUUM marked all-visible: watch Heap Fetches.

A function or cast on the column (created_at::date, a numeric bind on a bigint) stops the index search: keep the bare column on one side, or index the expression. Low-selectivity conditions are rightly scanned; partial indexes cover the rare values.
Every index is written on every insert and most updates: more WAL, more space. Choose indexes from pg_stat_statements and drop the ones pg_stat_user_indexes says are unused.

quiz.q: A query has `WHERE merchant_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50`. Which index serves it best?
options: (created_at, merchant_id)
(merchant_id, created_at)
Two separate indexes, one on each column
(merchant_id) INCLUDE (created_at)
quiz.why: With merchant_id first, merchant 42's entries are contiguous and already in created_at order, so the scan seeks to 1 September and reads 50 entries with no Sort. With created_at first, the scan reads every merchant's entries from 1 September on and checks each. INCLUDE columns are not sorted, so (merchant_id) INCLUDE (created_at) still needs a Sort. Two single-column indexes can be combined with a bitmap, but the result must still be sorted.

quiz.q: EXPLAIN shows `Index Scan using merchants_pkey on merchants m (actual rows=1.00 loops=2500)` with `Buffers: shared hit=7500`. What did the node do?
options: It read 1 row in 7,500 pages
It ran 2,500 times, found one row each time and read 3 pages per run
It ran once and returned 2,500 rows
It estimated 2,500 rows and found 1
quiz.why: rows is an average per loop, so the node produced 2,500 rows in 2,500 runs: the inner side of a nested loop. Buffers are a total over all loops, 3 pages per run, one descent of a small B-tree plus one table page. Estimates appear in the cost=... part, not in actual rows.

quiz.q: The login service runs `WHERE lower(email) = lower(?)` and customers has a UNIQUE index on email. The plan is a Seq Scan. What is the fix?
options: ANALYZE customers, so the planner sees the index
Rewrite it as `WHERE email = ?`
CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email))
Raise work_mem
quiz.why: The index is sorted by email, not by lower(email), so it cannot be searched for the lowered value; fresh statistics change nothing. Rewriting to email = ? changes the meaning, since stored emails may have capital letters. An index on the expression is sorted by exactly the value the query compares.

quiz.q: You add an index on payments(status). `SELECT sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded'` still runs as a sequential scan. Why?
options: 93% of rows match, so reading the table straight through is cheaper than following 930,000 index entries
Indexes cannot be used on text columns
The planner needs a hint to use a new index
sum() always needs a sequential scan
quiz.why: The planner compares estimated costs. Fetching nearly every row through the index means visiting nearly every page anyway, in a worse order, so the Seq Scan wins. The same index is used for status = 'pending', 1% of rows, and a partial index on the rare value is the better tool. PostgreSQL has no optimizer hints, and B-trees work on text.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: a heap row carries `t_xmin` and `t_xmax`. Right after a bulk load into a new table, a query that an INCLUDE index fully covers runs as a Bitmap Heap Scan over 39 table pages. After `VACUUM`, the same query is an Index Only Scan with `Heap Fetches: 0`. What did VACUUM change?
options: It moved the INCLUDE columns from the heap into the index
It refreshed the planner's statistics, which were missing
It rebuilt the index in sorted order
It set the all-visible bit for every page in the visibility map, so PostgreSQL no longer has to check each row's t_xmin and t_xmax in the heap
quiz.why: Index entries carry no visibility information: whether a row version is visible lives in its heap tuple. An index-only scan may skip the heap only for pages the visibility map marks all-visible, and only VACUUM sets those bits. Before it, every row would need a heap visit anyway, so the planner chose the bitmap scan. The INCLUDE columns were in the index from the start, and ANALYZE had already run without setting a single bit.

flashcards.front: PostgreSQL vs InnoDB: what does a secondary index entry point at?
flashcards.back: PostgreSQL: the row's ctid in the heap, so a lookup is one descent plus one heap page. InnoDB: the primary key, so a lookup descends the clustered index a second time.

flashcards.front: In EXPLAIN ANALYZE, what is rows=1.00 loops=14?
flashcards.back: One row per run, 14 runs: 14 rows in all. rows is always an average per loop.

flashcards.front: Index Cond or Filter: which one uses the index to search?
flashcards.back: Index Cond. A Filter is tested row by row after the rows were read; Rows Removed by Filter counts the waste.

flashcards.front: Column order rule for a multicolumn B-tree index?
flashcards.back: Equality columns first, then the one column you range over or sort by. PostgreSQL 18 skip scan relaxes it only when the leading column has few distinct values.

flashcards.front: Why does `WHERE created_at::date = '2026-09-01'` miss an index on created_at?
flashcards.back: The index is sorted by created_at, not by the computed date. Write a half-open range on the bare column instead.

flashcards.front: What makes an Index Only Scan possible?
flashcards.back: Every column the query needs is in the index (key or INCLUDE), and the visibility map marks the pages all-visible. Heap Fetches counts the exceptions.

flashcards.front: Where do you find the queries that most need an index?
flashcards.back: pg_stat_statements, ordered by total_exec_time: calls, mean time and pages per normalized query.

terms.plain: An index whose leaves hold the rows themselves, as InnoDB's primary key does, so the table is the index.
Two bits per heap page; the all-visible bit, set only by VACUUM, lets an index-only scan skip that page.
Reading a table's pages from first to last and testing every row.
One 8 KB page as EXPLAIN counts it: hit if it was already in PostgreSQL's memory, read if it came from the operating system.
A condition the database can use to search an index: the bare column compared with values computed beforehand.
An index that holds every column a query needs, often through INCLUDE, so the query can run as an Index Only Scan.
An index over only the rows that match its WHERE clause, such as status = 'pending'.
PostgreSQL 18's way to use a multicolumn index without a condition on its leading column, by searching once per leading value.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate added an index on payments(created_at) for the daily settlement report, which filters with `WHERE created_at::date = :day`, and the report is as slow as before. Explain what is happening and what you would change, and how you would prove the fix with EXPLAIN.
explain_back.answer: The index is a sorted copy of created_at values. The report compares created_at::date, a value computed from each row, and the index is not sorted by that, so PostgreSQL cannot seek to the day's first entry. It either scans the table or reads the entire index and casts every value, and the plan shows the condition as a Filter with hundreds of thousands of rows removed: on the course's large data set that was 2,739 pages for one day. An index on the expression would fix the search, but created_at::date depends on the session time zone, so PostgreSQL refuses to index it. The clean fix is to rewrite the condition as a half-open range on the bare column: created_at >= :day and created_at < :day + 1, with the boundaries computed in UTC or the business time zone in the application. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) then shows an Index Scan or Index Only Scan with both bounds under Index Cond, no Filter on created_at, and buffers in the tens: 13 pages in the course's run. I would check it on production-sized data, because on a small table every plan looks fast.

deeper.body:
BRIN is a different kind of index for tables whose physical order follows a column. It stores only the minimum and maximum of each range of pages, 128 pages by default, so a BRIN index on `payments(created_at)`, whose rows were inserted in time order, is 24 kB instead of 21 MB, and a time-range query skips every page range that cannot match. It is useless when the order is mixed, as it is for `ledger_entries.created_at` in the large data set, which was loaded by entry type. `pg_stats.correlation` tells you which case you are in: 0.999 for payments.created_at, 0.314 for the ledger's. Near 1 or -1 suits BRIN.

GIN, from the SQL track's lesson on JSONB, is an inverted index: one entry per key or value found inside a document or array, each with the list of rows that contain it. It answers `@>` and friends, and it pays for that on writes; its fastupdate buffer of pending entries hides part of the cost until VACUUM or a full buffer merges them.

The planner's estimates come from statistics that `ANALYZE` (and autovacuum) collect: a sample of each column's values, its most common values, a histogram, the number of distinct values. When two columns are correlated, say merchant_id and country, the planner multiplies their selectivities as if they were independent and underestimates. `CREATE STATISTICS` on the pair fixes that. Lesson 10 of this track, Query optimization and cardinality estimates, builds the estimator itself.

In production, `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes to the table for as long as it runs. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` does not, at the price of two passes over the table and the rule that it cannot run inside a transaction block, so a Flyway migration that uses it must be marked non-transactional. If it fails halfway, it leaves an INVALID index behind that you must drop.

`auto_explain` logs the plan of every statement slower than a threshold, with `auto_explain.log_analyze` for actual rows. It is the way to catch the plan of a query that is only slow in production, at 3 a.m., with that day's data.
